title: What is known about 1RB0LD_1RC0RD_1LA0RC_1RE1LB_1LF0LA_---0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_1RC0RD_1LA0RC_1RE1LB_1LF0LA_---0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open; only a first look has been taken. Two shift rules of its sweeps are proved in Lean for every length; no halt in the first 109 steps (C) and 107 (Lean, native_decide).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 29,507 cells have been visited and 17,521 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Two shift rules
claims.text: Rightward, C zigzags across 1 0 1 words, rewriting each into 1 1 0 in 7 steps (sweep_right); leftward, A crosses 1 1 0 words, rewriting each into 1 0 0 (sweep_left_A); for every n and every surrounding tape. Both occur in the run (22,783 and 7,892 times with n ≥ 3 in the first 3·106 steps).

claims.title: Two shift rules
claims.text: Rightward, C zigzags across 1 0 1 words, rewriting each into 1 1 0 in 7 steps (sweep_right); leftward, A crosses 1 1 0 words, rewriting each into 1 0 0 (sweep_left_A); for every n and every surrounding tape. Both occur in the run (22,783 and 7,892 times with n ≥ 3 in the first 3·106 steps).

claims.title: Words and sweeps
claims.text: At the moments the head stands at the left end (state B), the tape cut into words 1^i 0^j uses only 1 1 0, 1 0, 1 0 0 and 1 1 0 0 (plus a short piece at the start); near the left end the word 1 0 · 1 1 0 · 1 1 0 0 repeats five times. The head sweeps from the left end to a turning point inside the tape and back; the turning point moves irregularly from sweep to sweep; the right end stopped growing (228 cells right of the start after 109 steps).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. F is entered only from E reading 0 and E only from D reading 0 or F reading 1, so a halt needs the leftward E/F zigzag (which crosses 0 1 words) to meet two 0s in the wrong phase.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine zigzags: it moves a cell or two forward and one back, over and over, rewriting the words its tape is made of. Its sweeps run from the growing left end to a turning point inside the tape that wanders from sweep to sweep. Only a first look has been taken so far.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 29,507 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Shift rules of the sweeps, proved in Lean for every length.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.499). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 29,507 cells (21,488 left of the start, 228 right), with a density of 1s of 0.594.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Words and zigzag sweeps
html: Cut the tape into words of the form 1^i 0^j. Whenever the head is at the left end (state B), only four words occur: a = 1 1 0, b = 1 0, c = 1 0 0 and d = 1 1 0 0. After 7,187 steps the tape reads b a3 b d b a d b a d b a d b a d b a d b a12 b (a3 = a a a); after 3·107 steps it begins b a3 b d b a d b a d b a d b a d b a d b a4 b d ... and goes on for thousands of words in an irregular mix.

The head never runs straight: going right, C reads 1 0 1, writes, steps back, and comes forward again, 7 steps per word, leaving 1 1 0 behind (sweep_right); going left, A turns 1 1 0 into 1 0 0 (sweep_left_A), with other short zigzags in between. Each sweep runs from the left end to a turning point inside the tape and back, and the left end grows by about 5 cells per sweep. The turning point wanders from sweep to sweep, so the inner part of the tape behaves like a counter with an irregular carry; its exact rule has not been worked out.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The halting transition is F reading 0. F is entered only from E reading 0, and E from D reading 0 or from F reading 1: going left, E and F alternate across 0 1 pairs (E on a 0, F on a 1). The machine halts only if that leftward zigzag meets two 0s in a row in the wrong phase.

sections.heading: What is proved
html: Lean, kernel: the halting configurations, no halt in 10,000 steps (lean/Blank.lean), and the shift rules sweep_right and sweep_left_A for every length (lean/Passes.lean). Lean, native_decide: no halt in 107 steps. C: no halt in 109 steps. Everything else on this page is observation.

summary: A zigzagging bouncer: the head sweeps between the growing left end and a turning point inside the tape, rewriting words 1 0 1 into 1 1 0 going right and 1 1 0 into 1 0 0 going left; the turning point moves irregularly; open (first look only).
